articles.title: Turkish lawmakers approve defence pact with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia
articles.text:
Turkish legislators on Thursday ratified a defense cooperation agreement among Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia as Riyadh seeks increased regional support in its conflict with Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
The vote also came as countries in the region remain anxious about the prospects of a new escalation in the US-Iran war, which would likely spill over into neighboring countries. During previous rounds of fighting, Iran has lashed out at US-allied Gulf Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia.
The 16-article Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed in August, commits the three countries to regard an attack against one as an attack on all three, to work together to deter threats and deepen military cooperation, share intelligence and strengthen defense industry ties.
It was approved by 279 votes to 119 in the 600-seat parliament, despite objections from opposition parties who argued that the agreement could embroil Turkey in regional wars and put Turkish soldiers in harm’s way.
“They brought this agreement to send Turkish soldiers to the deserts of Yemen,” said Murat Emir, deputy leader of opposition New Party lawmakers. The loss of Ottoman soldiers in early 20th century conflicts in Yemen looms large in Turkish cultural memory.
Fuat Oktay, chairman of parliament’s foreign affairs committee and a member of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling party, said Turkey would “not be drawn into an uncontrolled process against its will.” He added that the deployment of troops would only be possible with future parliamentary approval.
The Turkish officials have said Ankara is considering sending military assistance to Saudi Arabia but insist that the agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops would be deployed to fight in Yemen or to attack the Houthis.
Turkish troops, backed by a rapidly developing defense industry, make up the second-largest military in NATO. Any deployment of Turkish troops would require a separate approval by Turkey’s parliament.
Turkish and Pakistani officials have stressed that the agreement does not target Iran or any other country.
The agreement was signed in the Saudi holy city of Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Erdogan and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. It is seen as part of Saudi Arabia’s efforts to reduce its dependence on the United States and diversify its security partnerships.
The deal showcases how close relations between Saudi Arabia and Turkey have grown, after being highly strained just a few years ago, including over the killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in Istanbul by Saudi operatives.
Ministers from the grouping have already met twice – in Istanbul and in Riyadh – while high-level delegations from the three countries held talks in Tehran last month to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war.
During their meeting in Riyadh in September, the three countries agreed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defense commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia. They did not elaborate.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said last week during a conference in Bahrain that discussions were underway about Syria joining the pact. Syria has close relations with both Turkey and Saudi Arabia, and joining the pact could give it more strategic leverage against Israel, which has launched strikes in Syria and occupied part of the country’s south since a rebel offensive ousted former Syrian President Bashar Assad in December 2024.
A Turkish official confirmed that the issue of Syria joining is being discussed, but said the existing members of the pact were focused on efforts to “institutionalize” the agreement and until they do, “there will be no question of any third country participation.” The official was not authorized to publicly discuss the issue.
According to the agreement, the grouping’s secretariat will be based in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. He will serve a three-year term.
The pact binds the parties for 10 years, after which they would need to provide a three-month notice to leave.

articles.title: End of Maoist terror victory of right policies and strong political will: Modi
articles.text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said the end of Maoist terror and Naxal menace was a victory of the country’s right policies and a strong political will.
“Our government took decisions which dealt very big blows to the funding of Naxals and secessionists,” Modi said, while celebrating Diwali with security personnel at a CRPF camp in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar district.
Decisions taken by the government destroyed fake currency nexus and choked the supply line of Naxals and secessionists, Modi said.
“The fight against Maoist terror and Naxalism was not easy; there was a time when more than 230 districts in nearly 20 states were affected by Naxalism,” he said.
To move the country forward, the nation’s enemies must be crushed with unwavering determination and a well-planned strategy, Modi said.
“The lack of political will that the country had faced was addressed in 2014, when you gave this Pradhan Sevak the opportunity to serve Mother India,” Modi said.
For the first time in 47 years, not a single CRPF jawan lost his life in the line of duty over the past year, he said.
Bastar, long known as the epicentre of Left-Wing Extremism (Naxalism) in Chhattisgarh, has undergone a major transformation following aggressive counter-insurgency operations, massive surrenders, and development push.

articles.title: Battlefield 2042 Immortalises Player’s Legendary RendeZook
articles.text:
One of the most iconic stunts in Battlefield history was pulled off by a player many years ago. This stunt was recently recreated by developers DICE in the official reveal trailer for Battlefield 2042 and the player who created the most well-known version of it was surprised to see himself being paid homage to.
This stunt, often referred to as the RendeZook, involves a fighter pilot ejecting from their plane mid-air, performing a 180 turn and shooting the enemy fighter with a rocket launcher. You then have to get back into your plane.
This is very difficult to pull off. If you miss the plane or fail to fully destroy your opponent you will be stuck floating in the air with no way to get back down. Usually resulting in a dramatic fall or embarrassing death.
While this stunt was first seen in Battlefield 1942 when players would try to eject mid-loop, attack their enemies with their bazooka and get back into their planes.
The most well-known version of it in modern times was done by Anders Lodahl, (known in the gaming community as Stun_gravy) in Battlefield 3. He used his RPG to destroy the enemy fighter chasing him while he ejected from his moving fighter jet and got back into his jet.
This really captured the Battlefield community’s attention and helped make the term RendeZook (shortened from rendezvous and bazooka) popular. It became a benchmark for amazing mid-air stunts. Players have tried to do their own versions in various Battlefield games. However the biggest surprise came in June 2021 when DICE released the official reveal trailer for Battlefield 2042.
During the jet chase, a player ejected from their fighter, shot their enemy with their rocket launcher and got back into their jet mid-air. This was definitely an example of the RendeZook and long-time fans instantly knew what was happening.
Stun_gravy was surprised to see himself being paid homage to. He watched the trailer and was unaware that DICE had added in a version of the stunt he is known for. This video shows how excited and emotional he was to see a stunt he did being added into an official Battlefield cinematic.
This was a really special moment as the developers had decided to pay homage to something that came from the community’s creativity. The RendeZook is just one example of why the Battlefield franchise has been so unique. The huge maps, planes, vehicles and open combat areas mean creative players can try new and unusual strategies.
However, DICE paying homage to the stunt in Battlefield 2042 is also a sign of appreciation to the community who helped make the franchise what it is today.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE
articles.summary: One of the most iconic stunts in Battlefield history was pulled off by a player many years ago. This stunt was recently recreated by developers DICE in the official reveal trailer for Battlefield 2042

articles.title: Indian Navy Targets Four Advanced Radar Technologies
articles.text:
The Indian Navy have identified four key areas where radar systems will be developed internally: Multifunction Phased Array Radars, Synthetic Aperture Radars (SAR), Low Probability of Intercept (LPI) Radars and Millimetre wave radars.
There will be a focus on developing solid state radar systems with electronically steered arrays, digital processing and fiberoptic links.
Multifunction Phased Array Radars
Radars in this category are a key area of development for the Navy. Rather than mechanical arrays these radars allow the radar beams to be quickly steered using electronically steered arrays.
This means that the radar can do multiple functions depending on how it is designed to interact with the ships combat management system. This could be search, tracking and engagement quality tracking. With warships becoming more active in contested environments it is an increasingly important feature to be able to detect and track targets such as aircraft, missiles and other threats. How well the radar will perform will depend on the power output, antenna design, digital processing and integration.
Synthetic Aperture Radar
The second area of development is Synthetic Aperture Radar. SAR uses the motion of the radar to create a large aperture effect. This provides high quality images.
As SAR does not use optics it can be used during the night. Based on the frequency it is operating on SAR can provide useful images even when there is cloud cover.
Within naval systems SAR can be used for maritime awareness, coastal awareness and intelligence gathering. How it can be used will depend on what the radar is being deployed on (airborne, spaceborne or other) and the overall sensor suite.
Low Probability of Intercept Radars
Low Probability of Intercept Radars are another key area of development. The aim here is to make it harder for an enemy to detect, categorise and attribute the radar emissions.
This can be achieved by controlling the transmit power, waveform, frequency hopping and signal processing. How effective it is will depend on how the radar is designed and the enemy electronic support capabilities.
This could be used on naval platforms if they are fighting against enemies with advanced electronic warfare and sensing capabilities. However, LPI does not mean they cannot be detected.
Millimetre Wave Radars
The last area of development is Millimetre wave radar. The very small wavelengths provide high resolution which can be beneficial. The benefits of this technology are increased reliability, quicker processing, less clutter and less false alarms. There will also be digital processing of radar signals closer to the antenna elements. This could simplify some areas of the signal chain. Overall the four areas of development provide multiple benefits.
By developing these radar technologies in-country we can give more control to Indian research organisations and industry over key areas of the sensor suite. This could lead to opportunities to work together between defence labs, electronics companies and naval platforms.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE
articles.summary: The Indian Navy have identified four key areas where radar systems will be developed internally: Multifunction Phased Array Radars, Synthetic Aperture Radars (SAR), Low Probability of Intercept (LPI)

articles.title: Pakistan Eyes Chinese SH-16A to Counter India’s K9 Vajra
articles.text:
Pakistan is reportedly looking to purchase China’s new SH16 155mm self-propelled howitzer to upgrade its aged artillery fleet. The Chinese system, featuring an automated artillery turret and tracked armour platform, could give the Pakistan Army a new option.
The SH16 has gained attention due to its automated artillery turret and modular design. This will help reduce workload for the soldiers. From imagery it can be seen that the system features a large unmanned turret, with a 155mm gun, mounted onto a tracked platform.
The standout feature of this system is the automated artillery turret. This will help reduce the amount of man power needed to run the howitzer when compared to traditional models. The new Chinese design features automation.
This system features a 155mm/52 calibre artillery gun. This type of gun is very popular in modern artillery forces due to being able to fire extended range munitions. The modular turret helps the system be adaptable.
Automation can help reduce the number of people needed to run the system, and help protect the crew by having more of the functions done inside the armour. This can help increase the rate of fire, however how effective it will be will depend on the ammunition handling system, fire control system and circumstances. Currently, Pakistan runs American M109 series tracked self-propelled howitzers. Pakistan runs multiple variants of the M109, which have been a key part of the Pakistan Army’s artillery. However, the older variants do suffer from some limitations.
Pakistan have already turned to Chinese technology with the purchase of the SH-15 155mm self-propelled howitzer. In 2019, Pakistan signed a contract with China to purchase 236 of the systems. This system uses a 6×6 truck.
The SH-15 offers increased mobility on roads, and is quick to deploy. However, if Pakistan were to purchase the SH16, it would offer increased mobility due to the tracked chassis. This would help allow the howitzer to move across rough terrain with the armour.
If Pakistan were to purchase the SH16, it could be used alongside the SH-15. This would help give the army more options.
This is relevant to India as they use the K9 Vajra-T, a tracked 155mm/52 calibre self-propelled howitzer, based on South Korea’s K9 Thunder.
India have already inducted 100 of these systems, and have ordered another 100. This would help give them increased mobility with their artillery support. The tracked system helps the howitzer move across tough terrain, whilst the protected nature means they can get closer to the front line.
If Pakistan were to purchase the SH16, it would give them a modern artillery platform. However, this would be misleading to just compare the two systems based on the calibre and automated turret. The protection, ammunition storage, rate of fire, range, fire control integration, reliability and mobility would all play a part.

articles.title: Rajnath Singh reviews preparedness of Trishakti Corps at Sukna
articles.text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday reviewed the operational preparedness of Trishakti Corps at Sukna in West Bengal on Saturday.
He was briefed on infrastructure development along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and the deployment of advanced military equipment and emerging technologies to enhance operational capabilities and combat effectiveness during his visit, according to a statement issued by the Defence Ministry.
The minister expressed satisfaction with the operational preparedness of the Corps and appreciated its contribution to nation-building through infrastructure development and community welfare initiatives in border areas, aimed at strengthening ties with local communities.
Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth; General Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Eastern Command, Lt Gen VMB Krishnan; and General Officer Commanding, 33 Corps, Lt Gen Man Raj Singh Mann were present on the occasion, along with other senior army officers.
Later, addressing the soldiers during Barakhana on the eve of Diwali, the Defence Minister commended their courage, professionalism and unwavering dedication towards safeguarding the nation’s frontiers under challenging operational conditions.
Underlining the importance of logistics in national security, he described Sukna and its surrounding region as a critical hub for the movement of supplies, weaponry, food, medical provisions and personnel to forward locations.
He stated that Sukna serves as a vital link in the security architecture of Eastern India and its geographical sensitivity necessitates round-the-clock operational readiness.
He added that the Government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is continuously working to strengthen supply chains and ensure that soldiers deployed at forward locations have access to all essential requirements.
Rajnath Singh highlighted that budgetary allocations for roads, tunnels, border infrastructure and modern equipment have been increased, with the nation steadily progressing towards ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’.
Highlighting the changing nature of modern warfare, the Defence Minister emphasised that security challenges are no longer confined to conventional exchanges of gunfire or artillery along the borders, but encompass hybrid warfare, proxy wars, cyber-attacks, drone incursions and information warfare.
He said that adversaries increasingly resort to spreading rumours through social media, monitoring sensitive locations using drones and attempting to compromise military systems through cyber-attacks.
He exhorted the personnel to remain vigilant and prepared to safeguard national security across all domains.
The minister reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to taking every possible step to boost troop morale and urged officers to spend quality time with soldiers whenever possible. Such interactions, he said, would foster a strong sense of belonging among personnel and reinforce their confidence that the Government and the entire nation stand firmly with them.
Describing the North-Eastern region as the ‘first edge’ rather than the ‘last edge’ of India, Rajnath Singh said that the region represents the beginning of the nation’s geographical and cultural landscape, as it receives the first rays of the morning sun.
Source: IANS

articles.title: ADA Begins Technical Evaluation of AMCA Prototype Bids
articles.text:
India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) project has entered a crucial stage of its procurement process, as the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) begins evaluating technical bids submitted by three Indian industry groups for prototype development and production. This is expected to take between three and four months, bringing us one step closer to identifying private-sector partners for India’s first indigenous fifth-gen fighter prototypes.
The groups involved are Tata Advanced Systems Limited, Larsen & Toubro led consortium with Bharat Electronics Limited and Dynamatic Technologies, and Bharat Forge led consortium with BEML and Data Patterns.
The Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) has now entered the technical bid evaluation stage after opening of technical bids. The three shortlisted industry groups have submitted their proposals by the closing date of October 30, 2026.
Tata Advanced Systems is entering the race alone bringing their expertise in aircraft structures and manufacture along with their current C-295 military transport aircraft build programme.
The Larsen & Toubro led consortium includes L&T, Bharat Electronics Limited and Dynamatic Technologies, bringing them a range of capabilities including L&T’s engineering and defence integration, BEL’s military electronics, radar and communications systems and Dynamatic Technologies’ aerospace manufacturing.
The final group of Bharat Forge led consortium includes BEML and Data Patterns, providing them with heavy engineering, precision manufacturing and defence electronics capabilities.
This is extremely important as whoever wins will have the responsibility of setting up the necessary infrastructure, processes and supply chain for a sophisticated stealth fighter aircraft. The selected DcPP will work alongside ADA who will provide design and management of the aircraft, to build five flying prototypes and one structural test airframe.
The prototype phase of the project will cost around ₹15,000 crore and will require a large amount of flight testing. The five flying prototypes will complete around 1,800 test flights during the programme. Over the next three to four months will be an important time period for the AMCA project as they look at the capabilities of each industry group.
The commercial bid evaluation will decide who will be the partner for one of India’s most ambitious defence aerospace projects.
This decision will also show if India’s private aerospace sector has the capability to manufacture a complex fifth generation fighter and set up the required capabilities for future combat aircraft.

articles.title: Enhancing Peacekeeping Priority For India In Seeking UNSC Election
articles.text:
India has said enhancing peacekeeping is a priority for it in seeking election to the Security Council with a firm commitment to bolstering the operations and protecting peacekeepers.
“It is because we regard peacekeeping as irreplaceable to this institution’s core purpose that India has identified it as a priority for our candidacy for the Security Council for the term 2028-29”, Colonel Tarunendra Pratap Singh, the military adviser at India’s mission, said on Thursday.
The elections to the Council for that term will be held next year.
“We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to UN peacekeeping and to a peacekeeping architecture that is better resourced, better protected, and more representative of the world it serves”, he said.
“India has deployed more than 300,000 troops across 50 missions, which makes us the largest troop contributor till date”, he pointed out.
Singh spoke at the annual debate on the comprehensive review of peacekeeping operations held at the Assembly’s Fourth Committee, which deals with special political and decolonisation matters.
He recalled India’s leadership when it was the Council’s president during its last term in ensuring the safety of peacekeepers and bringing those attacking them to justice.
During its presidency in August 2021, Singh said India piloted the Council resolution calling for accountability for crimes against peacekeepers, and it will continue its leadership on the issue.
The resolution said the targeted attacks on peacekeepers were a “major challenge” to UN operations and asked all countries hosting peacekeeping operations “to promote accountability for the killing of, and all acts of violence against United Nations personnel serving in peacekeeping operations”.
The UN’s blue helmets “today face asymmetric and technologically enabled threats and those who attack peacekeepers must be held accountable”, Singh said.
“India upholds the safety and security of peacekeepers as one of the most important aspects of peacekeeping”, he said, pointing out that 184 Indians have made the supreme sacrifice in UN operations..
Singh said that “troop and police contributing countries should have a structured voice in shaping the mandates” the Council sets for them.
It is necessary to have an institutional mechanism for consultations with troop and police contributing countries before mandates are adopted or reviewed, he said.
Peacekeeping operations are most likely to succeed when there is a “broader political process with a clearly envisioned political outcome and commensurate resources for peacekeepers”, he said.
“We should ensure capability enhancement and commensurate resources at the point of authorisation”, he added.
(IANS)

articles.title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
articles.text:
Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.

The missing electrons

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.

articles.title: Saudi KAAN Deal Could Open New Door for Pakistan against India
articles.text:
Saudi Arabia’s interest in the KAAN fifth generation fighter project could have wider implications for the country and could allow Pakistan to benefit financially.
Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ) have engaged in high level talks with Saudi Arabia regarding their involvement in KAAN. Reports from September 2026 showed that the negotiations were at an advanced stage. However, TUSAŞ officials said that the agreement would depend on Saudi demand and order quantity. In addition, they will want to know how much industrial involvement they want.
For Pakistan it could mean that the country can share the financial burden of the expensive next generation fighter project. However, there is no confirmed agreement that Saudi Arabia will pay for KAAN Fighters for the PAF.
The KAAN project is a large project for the Turkish aerospace industry aiming to give the Turkish Air Force a next generation combat aircraft with the goal of replacing their F-16s. It includes a sophisticated airframe design with stealth characteristics, mission systems, avionics and a long term goal of developing an indigenous engine.
If more partners get involved and offer some financial backing, large orders and/or local manufacturing then it will make the economics of the project look better. TUSAŞ General Manager Mehmet Demiroğlu said in February 2026 that there could be a small order for around 20 aircraft from Saudi Arabia. However, if they wanted to set up a final assembly line locally then they would need to commit to a much bigger order. Feasibility studies show that they would need to order a minimum of around 50.
With a Saudi partnership this could bring more finances into the project. If Saudi Arabia get involved in the project then Pakistan could benefit depending on if they can get an order in. Pakistan have already expressed an interest in KAAN. Previously Turkish officials said that Pakistani engineers were involved in certain parts of the project. Türkiye said “Discussions will begin with Pakistan to officially involve them in the fighter project.” This means that whilst Pakistan are interested in becoming an official partner in the project, it is still being discussed.
Being involved with engineers, an official development partnership, industrial involvement and/or an order for operational aircraft are all different engagements. They will all have different financial commitments and determine how much access Pakistan have to the technology.
The price of the aircraft is a key factor. Whilst it is estimated that KAAN will cost at least US$100 million per aircraft this will depend on what specification the aircraft is built to, how many are made, what support package is included, what weapons are fitted and what export deal is done. One option is Saudi Arabia could help make a larger multilateral deal viable. This could allow Pakistan to try and get an order in.
This could be an option for countries wanting to boost their defence industrial partnerships with Türkiye. However, Saudi Arabia also have aims to increase their local defence manufacturing so industrial involvement will be a key factor. Riyadh are also looking to the United States for their own fifth generation route. In September 2026 the US State Department approved a potential deal for the sale of 48 F-35 fighters to Saudi Arabia. This deal still needs to be approved by Congress. This gives Riyadh another large option.

articles.title: DRDO Seeks Wide-Band Data Recorder for Fighter AESA Radar
articles.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation has floated a tender to procure a Wide-Band Data Recorder and Replay System for its Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar systems for fighter planes, in a bid to improve its radar test and validation capabilities.
The tender, number GEM/2026/B/8148533, for a single unit of the recorder, was posted on the Government e-Marketplace, on November 3, 2026. Bids should be submitted by November 24 at 12 Noon. It requires an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of Rs 72 lakh. The estimated cost of the contract is ‘refer documents’.
The procurement is under the Data Logger Unit Storage category, and involves submitting a bid containing a technical specification dated October 12, along with the usual GeM bid documents.
Wide Band Data Recorders and Replay systems are usually used to collect high speed high volume electronic signals and data. For AESA radar fitted to fighter planes, they can be used to log and replay the radar.
This can be used to analyse how the radar performs in different modes, understand how the signals are being processed, and to analyse the electronic counter countermeasure capabilities. As the data has been logged, engineers can continually analyse it.
For modern fighter radars, that are required to work against a variety of aerial and ground threats in a challenging electronic environment, using the logged data can make debugging easier, improving software and validating the system. This is not a significant piece of equipment; however, it does demonstrate the need for special testing capabilities for the radar. With more indigenous AESA radars being fitted to India’s fighter aircraft, and complex electronic warfare capabilities being included, ground based instrumentation will play an important role in collecting and analysing the radar data.

articles.title: Doom delivers five minutes of terminal violence on an IBM mainframe
articles.text:
Can an IBM Z mainframe run Doom? Of course it can. The more interesting question is whether you can play it through a text terminal without ruining your eyesight.

WND Software's browser demo connects to an IBM Z mainframe over SSH using its terminal emulator. Wojciech Graj's DOOM-ASCII supplies the text-based carnage, replacing conventional graphics with colored characters. There's no sound.

It is, however, completely playable (although you might need to recalibrate your vision to work out what is going on, particularly with regard to distant objects). Sessions are limited to five minutes, with room for up to 50 simultaneous users, but we had no trouble getting in. ASCII also presented no issues once the game was in motion. This writer played the original shareware release on an Amstrad ALT386SX portable, so squinting at an indistinct demon felt reassuringly familiar.

That Doom can be persuaded to run on an IBM Z mainframe is not particularly noteworthy. The code has turned up everywhere from databases to PCB designers. Even the humble Pi Pico was roped into the fun.

Keeping the action playable through a text terminal is the more entertaining achievement. A year ago, an IBM consultant persuaded Doom to run on IBM Z and LinuxONE using VNC to bring the pixelated mayhem to life. Using a terminal emulator, while a neat demonstration of the capabilities of WND's software, is perhaps more an example of "because I can" masochism.

It's undeniably an enjoyable way to burn through five minutes. No installation or login required – just a willingness to shoot at punctuation. ®

articles.title: GTRE Seeks Advanced Altitude Test Facility for Fighter Engines
articles.text:
India needs state-of-the-art altitude engine testing and specialised manufacturing capabilities to develop and qualify next generation fighter jet engines locally, Dr S.V. Ramana Murty, Director, Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE), said.
Highlighting the need for an altitude test facility and testing capability at the part level, such as compressors, combustors and afterburners, Murty spoke at the Propulsion Systems session during the Defence Dialogue 2026 forum organised by the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA) in New Delhi.
Murty described the issues of compressor flutter and combustion screech, which cannot be adequately simulated using standard ground testing methods. These issues can affect stability of the engine and will therefore require specialised testing before the engine is approved for use.Murty explained that the issue of flutter can occur when operating at low Reynolds numbers and high Mach numbers. The Reynolds number is a dimensionless quantity describing the ratio of inertial forces and viscous forces in a fluid flow. The Mach number describes the velocity of air flow relative to the speed of sound.
These conditions can cause unusual airflow in the compressor section of the engine. As the engine operates at high altitude, the change in air density and aerodynamic loading can cause some unusual conditions.
Flutter is a self-excited aerodynamic instability where the blades of the compressor or other parts vibrate. This can cause excessive vibration if not managed correctly, causing fatigue in the engine.
Murty discussed the issue of screech which is a high frequency combustion instability caused by pressure vibrations in the combustion section. This is different to the noise produced in combustion and can cause severe acoustic loads to the parts of the combustor.
This will become obvious when testing at altitude.
This infrastructure would mean GTRE could test engines with more variety of conditions, compared to testing at ground level. In addition to an altitude facility, Murty stated there would also be a need for testing rigs for compressors, combustors and afterburners.
Having these parts means we can test sections of the engine. For example, compressors can be tested for aerodynamic performance. Combustors can be tested for combustion efficiency, pressure loss, temperature distribution and stability. Afterburners are also very important for military turbofans as they inject fuel to provide extra thrust.
This infrastructure would help engineers identify any weaknesses in their design early, minimising risk during development and improving reliability of future indigenous engines. Murty also listed three specialised manufacturing capabilities needed for advanced gas turbine production.
Firstly, a 20,000 ton hydraulic isothermal press. Isothermal forging means the material is formed at a controlled temperature, meaning difficult materials to work with at high temperatures can be formed with more accuracy. These materials are required in parts of the engine that operate at extreme temperatures.
Secondly, Electron Beam Physical Vapour Deposition (EBPVD). This is used to deposit thermal barrier coatings onto turbine parts. This helps to protect the metal surface from extreme temperatures.
Lastly, Linear Friction Welding. This is a welding technique that uses friction and pressure to join components together. This can be useful for producing complex turbine and compressor parts.

articles.title: PM Modi to celebrate Diwali with security officials in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar
articles.text:
) Prime Minister Narendra Modi will celebrate Diwali with the security officials posted in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar — a region historically affected by Maoism — highlighting how the situation in the area has transformed and development has gained momentum.
The Prime Minister said that he will salute the security personnel for their sacrifices and selfless service.
Taking to X, PM Modi said, “Heading to Bastar to celebrate Diwali with our brave security forces. This is an area where Naxalism once held sway, and now, development is flourishing.”
“I am going to salute our brave security personnel for their sacrifices, selfless service and unwavering devotion to the nation,” he added.
Every year, for over a decade, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has transformed his Diwali celebration into a national ritual, choosing to celebrate the festival of lights with the nation’s armed forces at its most challenging frontiers, plains or mountains.
In 2025, the Prime Minister celebrated Diwali aboard the indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant, positioned off the Goa-Karwar coast, marking his first time celebrating the festival of lights specifically with the Indian Navy.
Notably, he had commissioned the country’s first indigenous aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant, at Cochin Shipyard Limited on September 2, 2022.
His first Diwali as Prime Minister in 2014 set a high bar, celebrated with troops at the Siachen Glacier, the world’s highest battlefield. The following years saw him traverse the nation’s most sensitive border areas, with the Punjab border in 2015, the high-altitude post of Sumdoh near the China border in Himachal Pradesh in 2016, and the difficult terrain of the Gurez sector in North Kashmir in 2017.
He has also celebrated Diwali with the Defence forces in Harsil in Uttarakhand (2018), Rajouri in Jammu and Kashmir (2019), the legendary desert post of Longewala in Rajasthan (2020), Nowshera in Jammu and Kashmir (2021), Kargil in Ladakh (2022), Lepcha in Himachal Pradesh (2023), and Sir Creek in Gujarat (2024).

articles.title: Internet governance about to get its quadrennial stress test at ITU meeting
articles.text:
The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) kicks off its quadrennial plenipotentiary on Monday, and internet governance organizations are bracing in case the event becomes a forum for nation-states to try to challenge their roles.

The ITU is the United Nations' specialized agency for information and communication technologies, meaning its members are nation-states. The body's role is to facilitate international connectivity, which it does by managing radio spectrum, satellite orbits, and working on relevant technical standards.

Its key standards are pervasive. ITU-T X.509 sets out the rules of public key infrastructure. ITU-T E.164 governs telephone numbers. ITU-T H.264 and 265 define the video codecs used for most online streams.

The ITU's role is largely uncontested, yet its work gets very close to that of the organizations who work on technologies that make the internet work.

Those bodies include the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), which oversees the domain name system; and the regional internet registries (RIRs), which manage IP addresses. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) works on HTML, CSS, and accessibility.

Governments participate in work at those internet governance bodies but are just one voice among many and can't override the consensus-driven decision-making process they use, under a system which has come to be known as the multi-stakeholder governance model.

At a 2025 event called WSIS+20, the United Nations endorsed multi-stakeholder governance by deciding that its Internet Governance Forum (IGF) should become a permanent body. That decision effectively endorsed multi-stakeholder governance, and kept the ITU out of internet standards.

Yet the IGF hasn't met since WSIS+20, so it is yet to start operating meaningfully as a permanent body.

This year's ITU meeting is therefore a moment at which stakeholders can stress-test the delicate balance between the ITU, internet governance bodies, and the emerging IGF. Such a test could see ITU members try to have it pursue new fields that overlap with work performed by internet governance organizations.

This has already happened before. China tried to have the ITU work on "New IP" – a major revision to internet protocol, a technology the IETF manages.

In 2022, Russia and China backed a candidate for the ITU presidency who favored giving nations a stronger role in internet governance, potentialy by having the ITU take over some standards work. That candidate was not elected.

Ahead of next week's meetings, the Internet Society published a background paper that declared it is "actively challenging proposals that could affect the Internet's underlying technical architecture or increase fragmentation, as well as those that could affect connectivity, particularly for remote, underserved, and unserved communities."

The society is watching for resolutions on AI, quantum technologies, and other emerging areas that could embed specific technologies in ITU mandates. It also observes that decisions are yet to be made on which bodies should oversee governance of low-earth orbit satellite constellations, submarine cable resilience, and spectrum policy.

ICANN is also watching with interest.

"ICANN welcomes the recognition of the consensus-based WSIS+20 outcomes," the organization told The Register by email.

"At the same time, proposals that seek to expand the ITU's role in areas such as IP-based networks, the Domain Name System, management of Internet resources, and Internet-related public policy issues raise concerns about overlapping mandates and the creation of parallel processes that could affect the health of the Internet."

ICANN didn't point to any specific proposals that raise such concerns, and at ITU meetings most proposals – of which there are 278 this time around – are decided on consensus.

It is, however, possible for ITU members to amend proposals during meetings, leaving open the possibility of significant policy changes coming up for a vote during the 18 days the event occupies. ®

articles.text: The unraveling of the AI trade after the US midterm elections is forcing investors to rethink their Asia playbook, reviving demand for out-of-favor Chinese and Indian stocks as well as companies poised to benefit from easing inflation and trade tensions.Aberdeen Investments favors markets powered by stronger domestic growth, including India and Vietnam, and sees upside in Chinese technology firms. Hedge fund Lotus Asset Management is long Hong Kong equity futures, while Allianz Global Investors is looking at healthcare and consumer companies.Also Read: Bloodbath in Nasdaq, Kospi and Nikkei but why Nifty is an oasis of peace amid global rout135649455“I expect investors to diversify more broadly and reduce their concentration in the AI trade,” said Rajeev De Mello, global macro portfolio manager at Gama Asset Management SA. “This should be supportive of China and other markets where valuations are less demanding.”India could also benefit, although its dependence on imported energy remains a headwind, he added.China and India as HedgesHao Hong, chief investment officer at Lotus, said he is betting against oil and petrochemical firms and going long precious metals and Hong Kong equity futures.A Hong Kong gauge tracking mainland companies gained 5.2% last week, its best performance since March 2025.Meanwhile, some global investors are interested in using China’s onshore market exposure as a diversifier to their AI-heavy portfolio, according to Jason Lui, head of Asia-Pacific equity and derivatives strategy at BNP Paribas SA.Also Read: $5 billion in 5 days! Why FIIs are suddenly shopping Indian stocks non-stop this DiwaliIndia’s appeal, meanwhile, has grown as oil prices declined on expectations of an earlier end to the Iran war, easing a key pressure point for the energy-importing economy. The market’s lack of AI exposure is also now seen as an advantage.135649462LOGOS Asset Management’s chief investment officer Charlie Hong said he sold his shares in SK Hynix Inc., Samsung Electronics Co., Intel Corp. and Lumentum Holdings Inc. last month and has since boosted his Indian holdings with shares of new-age tech companies, financial firms and contract drug manufacturers.India’s benchmark Nifty 50 gained 8.6% last week. registering its best week since 2021, as overseas investors returned in force. Foreign funds poured a net $1.9 billion into local shares last week through Wednesday.The sudden shift has kept market participants busy. Utkarsh Singh, a Mumbai-based senior manager at SBI-SG Global Securities Pvt., started taking calls from clients in Singapore as early as 6:30 a.m. Friday and continued fielding queries late into the day as Indian stocks rallied.“Foreign investors are suddenly pouring in,” Singh said. “I have taken more calls from foreign funds this week than I have all year,” he said. “I think we will see more inflows.”Before the latest gains, key benchmarks in India and China had ranked among the world’s worst-performing stock indexes this year through October.Going Beyond AIBeyond China and India, investors are also taking a fresh look at previously overlooked corners of Asian markets that offer value and less exposure to the AI boom.While defence and financial stocks could underperform, healthcare and consumer staples firms may get a boost, Allianz Global Investors’ chief investment officer for public markets Michael Krautzberger and strategist Liam Wash wrote in a recent note.In Korea, Fidelity’s long-only portfolio manager Dale Nicholls said he sees early signs of rotation beyond the semiconductor heavyweights, particularly among domestic pension funds.“Consumption-related areas stand out, spanning sectors from wellness through to some of the K-pop entertainment agencies” and Korea’s beauty and cosmetics industry, he said.At hedge fund ACG Management Pte., managing director Hui Ling Loh said Korea’s consumer stocks including retailers, cosmetics, food and beverage are benefiting from the perception that they are largely domestically oriented and face limited tariff and policy risks from the US.Phillip Wool, head of portfolio management at Rayliant Global Advisors, said he sees opportunity in Korea and Taiwan, “but it’s going to be beyond the highest-profile chip stocks that have run up so much and are now subject to so much unease.”One stock Wool likes is LG Electronics Inc., which he holds in his active emerging-markets exchange-traded fund. The company sells a lot of TVs, refrigerators and washing machines in the US, which “could be a catalyst for some upside as tariff pressure eases,” he said.The prospect of less isolationist US trade policies has also raised investor confidence in auto firms including Japan’s Toyota Motor Corp. and South Korea’s Hyundai Motor Co.Not everyone is ready to abandon AI. Some investors say the selloff may offer an opportunity to buy the dip, given the sector’s longer-term growth prospects.But for now, caution remains the prevalent mood.Foreigners will likely continue to sell Asia’s AI “picks and shovels” stocks, said Manishi Raychaudhuri, chief executive officer of Emmer Capital Partners Ltd. “India and China are the only two large liquid markets offering a considerable array of non-AI exposures.”

articles.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
articles.text:
I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake.

To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers.

Things that were fun to get right:

- Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes.

- Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities.

- Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real.

Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io.

Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!
